answers.java_tx_design: My first three years were on a tax agency's audit case-management system, in Java. When an auditor opened a new case, the create-case endpoint wrapped a call to our external notification service — the one that emails the taxpayer — inside the same transaction as the case insert, because it was convenient to roll both back together on failure. Notification calls could take 2-4 seconds under load, and that held a row lock on a shared case-sequence table the whole time, which blocked other auditors from opening new cases during busy mornings. I moved the notification call outside the transaction, publishing a 'case created' event to a queue instead and letting a separate consumer send the notification with its own retry logic. Case creation went from occasionally queuing behind other opens for several seconds to consistently under 100ms.
answers.java_ops: On that same system, we had periodic OOM kills on Kubernetes during month-end audit reporting. Heap dumps showed a report-generation path loading entire result sets into memory as Java objects instead of streaming. I rewrote it to page through the query and stream rows to the output, which cut peak heap usage roughly in half for that path. Separately, our connection pool was fixed at 25 and I noticed through pool metrics that report generation held connections for the entire report duration, sometimes over a minute, starving the rest of the service. I moved report generation to use a dedicated smaller pool separate from the transactional one, so a slow report couldn't take down the interactive endpoints anymore.
answers.rust_readiness: I've run a production Rust service for about four years now: real-time validation and fraud scoring for tax return submissions, replacing a Java service that couldn't hold our latency target once volume grew. We peak around 1.2 million submissions a day during filing season with a 50ms p99 SLA. The Java version was sitting at about 220ms p99 under that load, mostly GC pauses from allocation-heavy scoring logic. The Rust rewrite of just that scoring path — not the whole system — got us to about 18ms p99, and per-pod memory went from around 4GB heap down to roughly 300MB resident. Early on we had a production panic from an unwrap on a None value in a rarely-hit code path, which crashed the pod under load instead of degrading; we fixed the immediate bug and then audited the whole service for bare unwraps, replacing them with proper Result handling and adding fuzz tests on the input parsing. On boundaries: I'd never propose rewriting a whole system in Rust — you find the one latency-critical, well-isolated piece, measure it, and migrate that.
answers.rust_boundary: Based on how we actually did our own scoring-service migration: I'd start by measuring which part of the write path is actually hot — for us that was the scoring computation itself, not the database write, so that's what we moved. I'd keep the interface between Java and Rust as narrow as possible; ours is a gRPC call with a well-typed request and response, no shared database access between the two languages for that path. Before and after, I'd watch p99 and p999 latency, memory per instance, and error rate, plus run the new path in shadow mode against the old one on live traffic for a couple of weeks to confirm the outputs agree before cutting over for real. For data consistency during the transition, we kept the Java service as the source of truth for the case record and had the Rust service only return a score, never write state directly — that made rollback trivial if something went wrong.
answers.money_correctness: Our submission intake endpoint gets hit multiple times for the same return when a taxpayer's browser retries after a slow response, so duplicate detection matters. We use an idempotency key built from taxpayer ID, tax year, and a client-generated submission UUID, checked against a unique index before the scoring pipeline even runs. It broke once: during a deploy, a brief window where the old and new versions of the intake service were both running let about 90 submissions get two different UUIDs for what was really the same retry, because the client library regenerated the UUID on retry instead of reusing it — a client bug, but it exposed a gap in our key design. We caught it within about 40 minutes via a spike in our duplicate-submission monitoring dashboard, which compares submission counts against distinct taxpayer-year pairs. We fixed it by adding a secondary dedup check on taxpayer-year plus a content hash of the return data, and coordinated with the client team on making UUID reuse on retry actually reliable.
answers.incident_response: The unwrap-on-None panic I mentioned is the clearest incident. It hit a specific malformed input pattern that only showed up for about 0.3% of submissions from one particular tax-prep software vendor's export format. Pods started crash-looping under load, and our alerting caught the restart-rate spike within about 3 minutes. I was on-call, traced it to the panic via the crash logs within maybe 10 minutes once I had a stack trace, and had a hotfix — a guard around that specific parsing path — deployed within 35 minutes of the initial alert. I told my team lead and posted in our incident channel as soon as I had a working theory, not after I'd already fixed it, since other submissions were still failing while I worked. The postmortem's real change was the fuzz-testing effort across the whole input-parsing layer, which found two more latent panics before they ever hit production.
answers.process_skipping: During that panic incident, I skipped our normal review for the hotfix — a guard clause around the bad parsing path — because pods were actively crash-looping and every minute of the normal PR cycle meant more failed submissions during filing season. I posted in the incident channel what the change was and that I was deploying without review, before I actually deployed it, and opened the real PR right after for someone to look at once things were stable. Outside of that kind of live, money-affecting outage, I don't skip review — even when I'm confident in a change, the actual cost of a second pair of eyes is small compared to what a bad deploy costs during filing season specifically.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I once shipped a config change to the scoring service's timeout value that was more aggressive than I'd tested, and about an hour later noticed elevated timeout errors in our dashboards myself before anyone paged me. I reverted it and posted what happened in the team channel the same afternoon, including that it was my mistake and roughly how many submissions had gotten a slower fallback path because of it. I've done on-call for the scoring service for the whole four years I've run it, weekly rotation with two other engineers, and filing season pages are frequent enough that I don't think of on-call as separate from building the thing — you learn more about your own service's actual failure modes from a 3am page than from a design review. I've also mentored one junior engineer through their first eight months on the team, mostly around reading Rust compiler errors and our incident process.
answers.evidence_decision: When we were deciding whether to migrate the whole submission-intake path to Rust or just the scoring computation, I actually argued for the narrower scope myself, using latency breakdown data showing the scoring computation was 85% of our p99, while intake and persistence were already fast. One of our architects wanted the bigger scope, arguing it would be cleaner long-term. We reviewed the numbers together and the team decided on the narrow scope for the first migration, with the option to revisit intake later once we had production experience with Rust. I followed that decision and didn't push to expand scope on my own afterward — eighteen months later, once we had the operational track record, the team did decide to look at moving intake too, and I led that follow-up migration with everyone's buy-in rather than doing it unilaterally the first time around.
answers.own_contribution: In the scoring-service migration I described, my own part was the actual Rust implementation of the scoring logic, the gRPC interface design, and the shadow-mode comparison harness I built to validate outputs against the Java version before cutover. What was the team's: two other engineers built the deployment pipeline and the canary rollout tooling, and our SRE lead set up the pod-level memory and latency alerting specific to the new service, since that wasn't something I had deep experience with at the time. On the follow-up intake migration, my part was again the core Rust implementation; the team's part was redesigning the client retry contract to fix the UUID-reuse issue I mentioned earlier, which needed people with more context on the client side than I had.
answers.java_recovery: Before the Rust migration, a batch job on the case-management system that synced audit outcomes back to the main tax ledger failed partway through after a downstream service timeout, leaving about 340 cases over a 90-minute window with an outcome recorded in our system but not reflected in the ledger. I scoped it with a query comparing our outcome table against the ledger's last-sync timestamp for that window, which gave me the exact case list. I fixed it by re-running the sync for just those 340 cases, writing new sync records rather than overwriting the failed attempts, and verified by pulling the ledger's confirmation response for each case and checking it matched our outcome data. My first pass at scoping under-counted — I'd filtered on the job's own log timestamps, which lagged the actual failure by a few minutes, and found 15 more affected cases once I used the ledger's own timestamps instead.
answers.java_perf_change: Before we built the Rust scoring service, I spent about two months trying to get the Java version's p99 down through tuning alone, since a full rewrite wasn't approved yet. Profiling showed most of the time was in object allocation for intermediate scoring results. I rewrote the hot path to reuse buffers instead of allocating new objects per submission, which got p99 from around 340ms down to about 220ms — real, but nowhere near our 50ms target. I also tried switching the GC from G1 to ZGC hoping pause times would improve, but our heap was still growing fast enough that it didn't meaningfully help and added some CPU overhead, so I reverted that part. That ceiling is actually what got the Rust rewrite approved — the tuning numbers showed the JVM itself was the limit, not our code quality.
answers.rust_hands_on: The clearest one from the production scoring service: early on I had a shared cache of scoring rules that I wanted multiple tokio tasks to read concurrently, and I reached for a plain HashMap wrapped in an Rc<RefCell<>> out of habit from single-threaded code, which the compiler rejected because Rc isn't Send. I switched to Arc<RwLock<>>, which compiled, but under real concurrent load I found readers were getting blocked behind writers more than I expected because I was holding the write lock across an await point during rule reloads. I fixed that by cloning the data needed for the reload out of the lock, building the new version, and only taking the write lock for the final swap, which is a pattern I now use anywhere I've got a tokio task touching shared state.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move the case-management system's core business logic to Rust — it changes constantly as tax law and audit procedures change, and the team that owns it doesn't have deep Rust experience, so the migration cost would be ongoing, not one-time. That's different from our scoring service, which is latency-bound and stable once tuned. I did hold back an urge to rewrite the intake service fully in Rust right after the scoring migration went well — I was excited about the results and wanted to keep going. I measured the intake path's actual latency contribution first, found it was a small fraction of our overall p99, and realized the ROI wasn't there yet. I brought that measurement to the team instead of just proposing the rewrite, and we agreed to leave it in Java until the client retry-contract issue made it worth revisiting for its own reasons, which is the migration I mentioned we did do later, with agreement.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: During one filing season, our scoring service's fraud-flag count for a single day didn't match what the downstream audit-selection system received — we flagged 1,140 returns, they recorded 1,097, a gap of 43. I noticed it from a daily reconciliation dashboard that compares counts across the two systems, flagged within a few hours of the day closing. The cause was a timeout on our side during a brief network blip that caused 43 flag events to be dropped by the message queue before the downstream system's consumer could pick them up, since we weren't using a durable delivery guarantee on that particular topic. I corrected it by re-emitting the 43 flags as new events rather than trying to reconstruct the original timestamps, and switched that topic to at-least-once delivery with the downstream consumer deduplicating on our idempotency key. Took about two hours to isolate — I initially suspected a bug in our flag logic itself before the queue metrics pointed at dropped delivery instead.
answers.prod_data_verification: When validating the shadow-mode comparison harness for the scoring migration, I was tempted to just run the new Rust path against live submissions and eyeball whether the scores looked reasonable. Instead I built the harness to run the Rust path in read-only shadow mode on the same live traffic as the Java path, logging both outputs without letting Rust's output affect any real decision, and compared them offline. That caught about a dozen cases over two weeks where the two disagreed, all traced to a subtle floating-point rounding difference in how the two languages handled one particular scoring formula, which I fixed before cutover. If something genuinely needs real traffic to validate, shadow mode against live data without acting on the output is where I go before I'd ever let a new path make a real decision on its own.
